 The government is considering changes to the long-term capital gains tax on equities before Budget 2027. Here is the current 12.5% LTCG rate, why a cut is being discussed, and how much investors could save at 10%, 5% or 2% on gains of ₹ 2 lakh, assuming the ₹ 1.25 lakh exemption stays.
 Sheetal Goel Published 27 Oct 2026, 11:15 AM IST Prefer Livemint on Google Share via Advertisement Govt may restructure LTCG tax on equities in coming weeks: How much could investors save if rates fall to 10%, 5% or 2%? (AI-generated image for representational purposes only) AI Quick Read The government is considering changes to the long-term capital gains ( LTCG ) tax on equities. A decision might be taken in the coming weeks before the Union Budget in February 2027, Moneycontrol reported on Monday, citing sources familiar with the matter, including a government official.
 Advertisement “A decision on restructuring is expected soon,” an official told Moneycontrol . The official added that the government is comparing India’s LTCG tax rate with those prevailing in major economies.
 The report also mentioned that the government is examining whether LTCG paid by foreign investors should be calculated on gains made in dollar terms. Currently, capital gains are calculated in rupees.
 A reduction in the tax rate could lower investors’ tax liability when they sell equity investments at a profit. Here is what investors need to know.
 What is the current LTCG tax on equities?
 Currently, profits from listed equity shares and equity-oriented mutual funds are treated as long-term capital gains if held for more than 12 months.
 Investors pay LTCG tax at 12.5% on eligible gains exceeding ₹ 1.25 lakh in a financial year. Applicable cess and surcharge are levied separately.
 Advertisement Also Read | Gold, debt and equity ETFs: How mutual fund capital gains tax rules differ What is the context of considering an LTCG tax cut?
 In its Ecowrap report dated 12 October 2026, SBI Research suggested that, “The government must seriously look into anchoring hot money flows into the equity segment by extending the holding period to say 2-3 years and abolishing the long-term capital gains tax for equity.”
 Separately, according to a News on Air report dated 13 October, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said: “The Government is open to hearing suggestions on the removal of long-term capital gains tax during consultations for the upcoming Union Budget.” She made the remarks at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi.
 Also Read | Income Tax Department highlights key TDS deadlines in Oct, Nov: Details inside How much could you save if the LTCG tax rate falls?
 The following calculations illustrate the potential tax savings if the rate is reduced to 10%, 5%, or 2%, assuming the ₹ 1.25 lakh annual exemption remains unchanged and excludes cess and surcharge.
 Advertisement Annual LTCG from equity Taxable gain after ₹ 1.25 lakh exemption Tax at the current 12.5% At 10% At 5% At 2% 
 ₹ 1 lakh ₹ 0 ₹ 0 ₹ 0 ₹ 0 ₹ 0 
 ₹ 2 lakh ₹ 75,000 ₹ 9,375 ₹ 7,500 ₹ 3,750 ₹ 1,500 
 ₹ 5 lakh ₹ 3.75 lakh ₹ 46,875 ₹ 37,500 ₹ 18,750 ₹ 7,500 
 *Estimated figures before cess and surcharge
 Annual LTCG is the profit earned from selling eligible equity investments after accounting for the acquisition cost. For example, if your annual LTCG is ₹ 1 lakh, it falls below the exemption limit, so no LTCG tax is payable.
 If your gains are ₹ 2 lakh, the taxable amount is ₹ 75,000 after deducting the ₹ 1.25 lakh exemption. At the current 12.5% rate, the tax comes to ₹ 9,375. On ₹ 5 lakh in gains, the taxable amount is ₹ 3.75 lakh, resulting in tax of ₹ 46,875 at 12.5%.
 For annual LTCG of ₹ 2 lakh, ₹ 75,000 would be taxable after deducting the ₹ 1.25 lakh exemption. The tax payable under different hypothetical rates would be:
 At 10%: Tax payable would be ₹ 7,500, saving ₹ 1,875.
 At 5%: Tax payable would be ₹ 3,750, saving ₹ 5,625.
 At 2%: Tax payable would be ₹ 1,500, saving ₹ 7,875.
 No LTCG tax would be payable on any amount of equity gains, assuming the government abolishes the tax. These are hypothetical scenarios, not confirmed proposals. Investors should continue to calculate their tax liability using the prevailing rules until the government announces any changes.
